lect: Tongan (Tongatapu dialect in acoustic study; descriptive stress generalisation)
claim: Primary stress falls on the penultimate mora of the phonological word; secondary-stress assignment is morphology-sensitive and can be variable in loanwords.

source_forms.secondary_stress: depends on morphology; variable for loanwords

normalized_environment: PrimaryStress=penultimate μ of PWd; SecondaryStress morphology/loan-stratum sensitive
scope: background generalisation; study speakers from Tongatapu
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The paper's own secondary-stress stimuli all had secondary stress on the leftmost mora, but it explicitly warns that this does not exhaust Tongan secondary-stress patterns; loans can vary.
section: 1.1 Background information on the Tongan language

claim: The definitive accent is marked by reduplication of the final vowel of a noun phrase, which shifts stress because stress remains penultimate; the resulting sequence can make a previously long final vowel trimoraic.

source_forms.example: non-definite [tamaˈsiʔi kaaˈkaa] 'cunning boy' vs definite [tamaˈsiʔi kaakaˈaa]

normalized_environment: V#NP -> VV under DEF; lexical stress recalculates to penultimate μ
scope: summary of Anderson & Otsuka 2006 in Garellek & White introduction
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The trimoraic result occurs only in some configurations; the source says 'in some cases' rather than treating trimoraicity as universal under definitive accent.

claim: The status of so-called syllable fusion is explicitly contested: some analyses allow particular VV sequences to fuse into one syllable, analyses disagree about which sequences and conditioning environments, and another analysis claims fusion never occurs.

literature_positions: Churchward 1953 / Feldman 1978 / Poser 1985 / Schutz 2001: some VV fusion

normalized_environment: VV syllabification unresolved in source literature; do not encode fusion categorically
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The disagreement itself is the record. No particular VV inventory or environment is staged as established from this source.
table_figure: prose; footnote 1 also notes competing analyses of long vowels

claim: Unstressed vowels are not centralized or reduced in overall vowel-space size; all five vowels instead have lower F1 when unstressed than under primary stress, so stress conditions vowel realization without neutralizing vowel-quality contrasts.

source_forms.primary_vs_unstressed: all five vowels have higher F1 under primary stress
source_forms.interpretation: unstressed vowels raised in vowel space; no overall vowel-space reduction

formal_environment: V under primary lexical stress vs unstressed
normalized_environment: V -> lower articulation/higher F1 under primary stress; unstressed inventory remains contrast-preserving
scope: four female native Tongatapu speakers; laboratory word-list study
exceptions_or_counterexamples: F2 effects are vowel-specific rather than general, and lexical stress in the primary-stress stimuli is confounded with postlexical pitch accent; the authors flag that confound explicitly.
